children: STOCKHOLM--Volvo Car scrapped its full-year guidance after warning that challenges in its key Chinese and U.S. markets led to lower-than-expected third-quarter sales and a weaker outlook.

The Swedish car maker--which is majority-owned by China's Zhejiang Geely Holding Group--said the market developments will significantly impact third-quarter earnings and cash flow, beyond previously highlighted raw material, currency and amortization and depreciation headwinds.
"As a result of the increased market uncertainty, Volvo Cars has also taken the decision not to provide any updated short-term forward-looking statement."
Shares were 3.2% lower in early Stockholm trade and are now down 52% year to date.

The company had previously expected growth in Europe and a recovery in the U.S. to spur significantly stronger sales in the second half of the year from the first half. It had also guided to strong positive free cash flow in the late second half of the year which was expected to see cash flow end the full year at around break-even.
It said Friday it sold 141,609 cars in the third quarter, an 11% drop on year as sales in the Greater China region plunged 41%, while Americas saw a 14% decline.

Europe held up better, supported by strong demand and order intake for fully electric cars, it said. The automaker doesn't break out figures for Europe alone, but sales for the Europe and Rest of World region edged 2% higher.
"The market downturn in China showed no signs of easing, and the recovery in the U.S. premium segment remained below our earlier expectations," said Chief Commercial Officer Erik Severinson.
"This impacted our third-quarter sales, and the same challenging market conditions have led third-party analysts to lower their sales forecasts for the premium car market for 2026."

The global auto industry is grappling with a shrinking Chinese market that remains embroiled in a long-running price war. The number of model launches by domestic brands has ballooned, with manufacturers offering deep discounts to entice customers.

Volvo Car has opted to avoid entering the discount wars, though, sticking to a strategy of protecting its premium pricing--which it has previously acknowledged would have a negative impact on the number of cars it sells.

In the U.S., a federal program that offered up to $7,500 in tax credits for new electric and hybrid vehicles and $4,000 for used EVs ended last year, hitting demand for the vehicles, but Volvo Car had recently sounded a more optimistic tone of a recovery after registering sales growth in the country over the summer months.
Friday's news comes just weeks after the company said Skoda boss Klaus Zellmer will take over as its next chief executive no later than October next year.

That announcement came just after it laid out a fresh plan to drive sales growth and higher profitability that includes its largest-ever product push, with 13 new car model launches by the end of the decade aimed at doubling its market share.

After completing an 18 billion Swedish kronor ($1.79 billion) cost-saving plan in 2025, followed by additional measures to save a further 5 billion kronor earlier this year, the company is hoping a new model lineup will drive growth and strong positive cash flows over the long term, with an operating profit margin above 8%.
These targets remain intact, despite Friday's removal of short-term guidance, it added.
Further actions to improve and accelerate execution of its strategy are being undertaken, with details expected to be released alongside the company's third quarter report on Oct. 23.
